claims.text: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference.
claims.poster_quote: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and the introduction of the paper.

claims.text: The reference is produced by an annotation process in which people label items, disagree, and have those disagreements resolved by an aggregation rule.
claims.poster_quote: The reference is not a constant: it is produced by an annotation process in which people label items, disagree, and have those disagreements resolved by an aggregation rule.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The reference is the output of an annotation process: people labelled items, they disagreed, and a pipeline resolved those disagreements according to some rule.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in the introduction of the paper.

claims.text: A different rule applied to the same human labour can yield a different reference.
claims.poster_quote: A different rule applied to the same human labour can yield a different reference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A different rule, applied to the same human labour, yields a different reference.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in the introduction of the paper.

claims.text: The aggregation pipeline retained Annotator A in 98.7% of cases when the two annotators disagreed and the third pass did not fire.
claims.poster_quote: When the two annotators disagreed and the third pass did not fire, the pipeline retained Annotator A in 98.7% of cases.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: When the two annotators disagreed and the third pass did not fire, the pipeline retained Annotator A in 98.7% of cases.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.2 of the paper.

claims.text: The silent default affected 10.6% of prompts pooled.
claims.poster_quote: This silent default affected 10.6% of prompts pooled.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This occurred on 10.6% of prompts pooled.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Table 1 under the 'Silent' column.

claims.text: The silent default affected 16.5% of prompts in Arabic.
claims.poster_quote: This silent default affected 10.6% of prompts pooled and 16.5% in Arabic.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This occurred on 16.5% in Arabic.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Table 1 under the 'Silent' column for Arabic.

claims.text: Where adjudication did fire on disagreement, the delivered gold reproduced Annotator B about as often as Annotator A.
claims.poster_quote: Where adjudication did fire on disagreement, the delivered gold reproduced B about as often as A.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Where the third pass did fire on a disagreement, the delivered gold reproduced B about as often as A (42.3% and 38.5%).
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.2 of the paper.

claims.text: Delivered gold reproduces Annotator A’s complete span set on 83.4% of prompts.
claims.poster_quote: On the audited subset, delivered gold reproduces Annotator A’s complete span set on 83.4% of prompts.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The delivered gold reproduces Annotator A’s span set exactly on 83.4% of prompts.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: Delivered gold reproduces Annotator B’s complete span set on 76.1% of prompts.
claims.poster_quote: On the audited subset, delivered gold reproduces Annotator B’s complete span set on 76.1% of prompts.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The delivered gold reproduces Annotator B’s span set exactly on 76.1% of prompts.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: Delivered gold shows a +7.3-point skew toward Annotator A.
claims.poster_quote: On the audited subset, delivered gold reproduces Annotator A’s complete span set on 83.4% of prompts and Annotator B’s on 76.1%, a +7.3-point skew toward A.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: That is a skew of +7.3 points toward A, present in every language and ranging from +2.7 (Polish) to +12.9 (Swedish).
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: The preference occurs in every language and ranges from +2.7 points in Polish to +12.9 in Swedish.
claims.poster_quote: The preference occurs in every language and ranges from +2.7 points in Polish to +12.9 in Swedish.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: That is a skew of +7.3 points toward A, present in every language and ranging from +2.7 (Polish) to +12.9 (Swedish).
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: Reviewer gold reproduces Annotator A on 70.55% of prompts.
claims.poster_quote: Reviewer gold reproduces A and B on 70.55% and 70.51% of prompts, showing no pooled preference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The reviewer gold coincides with A on 70.55%.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: Reviewer gold reproduces Annotator B on 70.51% of prompts.
claims.poster_quote: Reviewer gold reproduces A and B on 70.55% and 70.51% of prompts, showing no pooled preference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The reviewer gold coincides with B on 70.51%.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: One reference contains a systematic positional preference created by the aggregation rule.
claims.poster_quote: Thus, one reference contains a systematic positional preference created by the aggregation rule, while the other does not.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The delivered gold reproduces Annotator A’s span set exactly on 83.4% of prompts and Annotator B’s on 76.1%. That is a skew of +7.3 points toward A.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.1 and Table 3 of the paper.

claims.text: All measurements come from one benchmark and one annotation pipeline.
claims.poster_quote: All measurements come from one benchmark and one annotation pipeline, so the method transfers but the numerical band does not.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Every measurement comes from a single annotation record, and the size of the effect depends on properties of that record.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 5.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The reviewer sample was documented as random.
claims.poster_quote: The reviewer sample was documented as random, but randomness could not be verified from the export.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The data-preparation record states the reviewed prompts were randomly selected.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 5.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The export contains no annotator identifiers, preventing separation of differences in skill from differences in convention.
claims.poster_quote: The export contains no annotator identifiers, preventing separation of differences in skill from differences in convention.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The export carries no annotator identifier, so we cannot separate a systematic difference in skill from one in convention.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 5.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset supports pooled conclusions but gives limited per-language power.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset supports pooled conclusions but gives limited per-language power, while the 135-prompt decontaminated subset is too small for firm conclusions.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: 2,628 prompts establish pooled effects but not confident per-language ones.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 5.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The 135-prompt decontaminated subset is too small for firm conclusions.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset supports pooled conclusions but gives limited per-language power, while the 135-prompt decontaminated subset is too small for firm conclusions.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: With n = 135 and 13 to 30 items per language every interval straddles zero, and the subset is far too small to detect an effect of the size we report on the full data.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.4 of the paper.

claims.text: The scored outputs are human annotation passes, not independently developed model systems.
claims.poster_quote: The scored outputs are human annotation passes, not independently developed model systems, so the magnitude and pattern of reference sensitivity for model predictions remain empirical questions.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The outputs we score are human annotation passes, not model predictions.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in the note on scope in the introduction.

claims.text: The sensitivity band is 6.3 F1 points under STRICT matching.
claims.poster_quote: For this benchmark, the band is 6.3 F1 points under STRICT matching and 5.2 under RELAXED matching.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Taking the upper 95% bound on the largest pooled reference-swap delta gives 6.3 F1 points under STRICT.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.5 of the paper.

claims.text: The sensitivity band is 5.2 F1 points under RELAXED matching.
claims.poster_quote: For this benchmark, the band is 6.3 F1 points under STRICT matching and 5.2 under RELAXED matching.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Taking the upper 95% bound on the largest pooled reference-swap delta gives 5.2 F1 points under RELAXED.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.5 of the paper.

claims.text: Using Annotator B’s less circular delta gives a stricter STRICT band of 3.4 points.
claims.poster_quote: Using Annotator B’s less circular delta gives a stricter STRICT band of 3.4 points.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The largest pooled delta belongs to A, whose score against the delivered gold is partly circular (Section 4.4); the same band computed from B’s delta gives 3.4 points instead of 6.3.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.5 of the paper.

claims.text: Every delivered-gold margin between the two annotators falls below the 6.3-point band.
claims.poster_quote: Every delivered-gold margin between the two annotators falls below the 6.3-point band, showing that several apparent performance differences are the same order as uncertainty introduced by reference construction.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Every delivered-gold margin between the two annotators under the delivered gold (2.83 pooled, magnitudes 1.46 to 4.59 across languages) falls below the 6.3-point band.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.5 of the paper.

claims.text: The retained record includes two independent annotator labellings, the aggregate shipped as delivered gold, a selective third pass used as adjudication, and an independent expert reviewer gold for 10.5% of the corpus.
claims.poster_quote: The retained record includes two independent annotator labellings, the aggregate shipped as delivered gold, a selective third pass used as adjudication, and an independent expert reviewer gold for 10.5% of the corpus.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The record retains up to four labellings per prompt: the redundancy that makes this study possible, and which most released datasets discard.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2 of the paper.

claims.text: Both annotator passes are present on 99.6% of prompts.
claims.poster_quote: Both annotator passes are present on 99.6% of prompts.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Annotators A and B labelled each prompt independently, both present on 99.6% of prompts.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2 of the paper.

claims.text: The delivered gold is identical to one annotator’s complete span set on 94.9% of audited prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The delivered gold is a selection rather than a merge: on 94.9% of audited prompts it is identical to one annotator’s complete span set.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On 94.9% of audited prompts the shipped reference is identical to one of the two annotator labellings.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and Section 2 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: After deduplication it holds n = 2,628 prompts.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains 350 Hindi prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Hindi 350.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains 630 Portuguese prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Portuguese 630.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains 339 Polish prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Polish 339.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains 341 Swedish prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Swedish 341.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains 623 Chinese prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Chinese 623.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The audited subset contains 345 Arabic prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The audited subset contains all four labellings for 2,628 prompts: Hindi 350, Portuguese 630, Polish 339, Swedish 341, Chinese 623, and Arabic 345.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Arabic 345.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The reviewer differs from the delivered gold on 22.0% of audited prompts.
claims.poster_quote: The reviewer differs from the delivered gold on 22.0% of audited prompts.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On it, the reviewer’s labelling differs from the delivered gold on 22.0% of prompts.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 2.3 of the paper.

claims.text: Holding the output fixed and changing only the reference moves pooled scores by 2.00–4.95 F1 points.
claims.poster_quote: Holding the output fixed and changing only the reference moves pooled scores by 2.00–4.95 F1 points and by as much as 7.55 points in one language.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Holding each annotator’s output fixed and scoring it first against the delivered gold and then against the reviewer gold, Annotator A scores 91.62 and 86.67: a difference of 4.95 points, 95% CI [3.23, 6.27]. Annotator B moves by 2.00 points, CI [0.26, 3.37].
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.2 and Table 2 of the paper.

claims.text: Holding the output fixed and changing only the reference moves scores by as much as 7.55 points in one language.
claims.poster_quote: Holding the output fixed and changing only the reference moves pooled scores by 2.00–4.95 F1 points and by as much as 7.55 points in one language.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: It is largest in Hindi (7.55 points, CI [4.90, 10.91]).
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.2 and Table 2 of the paper.

claims.text: The pooled interaction is +2.95 points.
claims.poster_quote: It also changes the comparison between outputs: the pooled interaction is +2.95 points, survives correction for multiple testing, and changes the Hindi margin’s sign.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Pooled, the interaction is +2.95 points, 95% CI [+1.97, +3.87].
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The pooled interaction survives correction for multiple testing.
claims.poster_quote: It also changes the comparison between outputs: the pooled interaction is +2.95 points, survives correction for multiple testing, and changes the Hindi margin’s sign.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Pooled, the interaction is +2.95 points, 95% CI [+1.97, +3.87], and survives Holm correction over all 14 tests we report.
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in Section 4.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The pooled interaction changes the Hindi margin’s sign.
claims.poster_quote: It also changes the comparison between outputs: the pooled interaction is +2.95 points, survives correction for multiple testing, and changes the Hindi margin’s sign.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The Hindi margin changes sign (Section 4.3).
claims.reason: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and Section 4.3 of the paper.

claims.text: The primary cause is an undocumented default that usually retained the first annotator when disagreement was not adjudicated.
claims.poster_quote: The primary cause is an undocumented default that usually retained the first annotator when disagreement was not adjudicated.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The cause is an undocumented aggregation default that usually kept Annotator A when adjudication did not fire.
claims.reason: Section 4.1 explicitly states that the primary cause is an undocumented aggregation default that usually retained Annotator A when adjudication did not fire.

claims.text: A benchmark score measures both a system and a reference.
claims.poster_quote: A benchmark score measures both a system and a reference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Our results say it measures a system and a reference, and that the second term is not small: larger than every margin observed in this paper.
claims.reason: Section 5.1 explicitly states that a benchmark score measures both a system and a reference.

claims.text: Reference sensitivity should be reported alongside the score.
claims.poster_quote: Reference sensitivity should therefore be reported alongside the score.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We suggest benchmarks report a reference-sensitivity band alongside the score.
claims.reason: Section 5.2 explicitly recommends reporting reference sensitivity alongside the score.

claims.text: Computing reference sensitivity requires no new annotation.
claims.poster_quote: Computing it requires no new annotation—only retaining the annotation record and scoring fixed outputs against more than one defensible reference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Computing it costs no new annotation, only keeping the annotation record instead of discarding it, and scoring against more than one reference.
claims.reason: Section 5.2 explicitly states that computing reference sensitivity requires no new annotation.

claims.text: The record contains 24,939 prompts after deduplication.
claims.poster_quote: After deduplication, the record contains 24,939 prompts, roughly 4,100 per language, from seven business domains and twelve task categories.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We study the annotation record of a production benchmark for PII span extraction across six languages (Hindi, Portuguese, Polish, Swedish, Chinese, and Arabic), holding 24,939 prompts after deduplication.
claims.reason: Section 2 explicitly states that the record contains 24,939 prompts after deduplication.

claims.text: The record contains roughly 4,100 prompts per language.
claims.poster_quote: After deduplication, the record contains 24,939 prompts, roughly 4,100 per language, from seven business domains and twelve task categories.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We study the annotation record of a production benchmark for PII span extraction across six languages (Hindi, Portuguese, Polish, Swedish, Chinese, and Arabic), holding 24,939 prompts after deduplication, roughly 4,100 per language.
claims.reason: Section 2 explicitly states that the record contains roughly 4,100 prompts per language.

claims.text: The record spans seven business domains and twelve task categories.
claims.poster_quote: After deduplication, the record contains 24,939 prompts, roughly 4,100 per language, from seven business domains and twelve task categories.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The export tags each prompt with one of seven business domains (finance, IT, insurance, travel, media, health, retail) and one of twelve task categories, such as summarisation, translation, and conversation.
claims.reason: Section 2 explicitly states that the record spans seven business domains and twelve task categories.

claims.text: Spans contain character start and end offsets plus one of 21 shared or 77 locale-specific types.
claims.poster_quote: Spans contain character start and end offsets plus one of 21 shared or 77 locale-specific types.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A span is a character start offset, an end offset, and one type, drawn from 21 shared and 77 locale-specific types.
claims.reason: Section 2 explicitly states that spans contain character start and end offsets plus one of 21 shared or 77 locale-specific types.
